clue.text: Like Elisha's way of dashing at things?

definitions.text: Like Elisha's way of dashing at things?

parts.words: Like Elisha's way of dashing at things?
parts.note: the prophet Elisha was mocked for having no hair on his crown, and charging in recklessly is to go at something without a hat on, so one word serves both

explanation.surface: A question about how the Old Testament prophet Elisha rushed into things.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2 Kings, children jeer at Elisha as 'thou bald head'; to go at something 'bald-headed' is an old idiom for rushing at it recklessly.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a hairless scalp, as Elisha had, and is also the idiom for charging in without caution.

clue.text: Just a little one, sweetheart?

definitions.meaning: a term of endearment for a loved one

explanation.surface: Someone asks a lover for just a small drink.
explanation.definitionFit: An infant is a little one, and the word is also an endearment for a lover.

clue.text: Tyrannizing many love awful grind

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, taken as many
O is love, a zero score in tennis

indicators.note: the word grind is made awful, its letters messed into a new order

explanation.surface: Tyranny means plenty of love turned into a dreadful slog.
explanation.walkthrough: To lord it over people is to domineer, hence this present participle.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting like a lord over others, domineering, is bullying them as a tyrant does.

clue.text: Peacock's impetuous passage to the front door

parts.note: headlong means rash, impetuous
a hall is the entrance passage of a house

explanation.surface: A peacock rushing down the corridor to the front door.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Love Peacock wrote the satirical novel of this name in 1816; 'Peacock' is not the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of Thomas Love Peacock's first novel, so it is Peacock's book.

clue.text: All memoranda initially revised in case he's forgotten

indicators.note: only the opening letters of All and memoranda are taken
in case is revised, its letters rewritten in a fresh order

explanation.surface: All notes are rewritten in case someone has forgotten.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with memory loss is one who has forgotten.

clue.text: Brought in income? 'ark at Edward!

parts.note: 'ark is dropped-aitch Cockney for hark, which means listen, as does 'ear for hear
Ned is a pet form of Edward

explanation.surface: A Cockney mocks Edward for having brought home some money.
explanation.definitionFit: Money brought in as income has been gained by work.

clue.text: Attempt at regicide at Inverness

definitions.meaning: a try or go at something
Macbeth kills King Duncan with a dagger at his castle at Inverness

explanation.surface: An attempt on a king's life in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare sets Macbeth's castle at Inverness, where Duncan is murdered with daggers.
explanation.definitionFit: A try is a 'have a go', and Duncan's murder was done by plunging a dagger.

clue.text: Polite circle embarrassed artist by artist

indicators.note: the word polite is embarrassed into disorder, its letters rearranged

parts.note: O is the shape of a circle

explanation.surface: A polite social circle is embarrassed by a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo was a Venetian painter whose son Giandomenico was also a painter, hence an artist fathered by an artist.
explanation.definitionFit: The family name is shared by the Venetian painter and his painter son, an artist born to an artist.

clue.text: Only fools obstruct the bosses

parts.note: to block is to obstruct
heads are leaders, bosses

explanation.surface: Only idiots would get in the way of their managers.
explanation.definitionFit: Dunces or dolts are thick-headed fools.

clue.text: Those who treat-or those they treat in pubs?

definitions.meaning: people who negotiate or haggle over terms
read as ..., people who gain something at the bar when a round is bought

explanation.surface: Those who stand drinks, or those for whom drinks are stood in pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Treat' first means negotiate (treat with an enemy), then buy someone a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Hagglers negotiate terms; split in two the word also suggests people who profit at a pub counter.

clue.text: How Noel might appear as a Great Dame

indicators.note: the letters of the name Noel might show up in a different order, signalled by appearing as something else

explanation.surface: Noël Coward imagined dressed up as a pantomime dame.
explanation.walkthrough: Dan Leno was a celebrated Victorian music-hall comedian famous for playing pantomime dames, a British Christmas theatre tradition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dan Leno was the most famous pantomime dame of the Victorian stage.

clue.text: Establishment of one with a seat in the country

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the seat is placed inside the word for the country

parts.note: a nation is a country, a people and its land
a stall is a theatre seat, or a seat in a church choir

explanation.surface: Someone who has a seat in the countryside, a landed gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to a country seat; the answer means setting someone up in office.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting up or putting in place, as of a priest in a stall, is establishing.

clue.text: Fight in the works

definitions.meaning: a fist fight or brawl, in old slang

explanation.surface: A punch-up on the factory floor.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxing bout is slang for a punch-up, and a factory is a manufacturing plant.

clue.text: Alpine climber uses a mug with beer

parts.note: a stein is a large beer mug
bock is a strong German lager

explanation.surface: A mountaineer in the Alps who drinks from a tankard.
explanation.definitionFit: The ibex, a wild mountain goat of the Alps, goes by this German name.

clue.text: They're not bitter-mouthed, being bitter at heart

definitions.text: They're not bitter-mouthed, being bitter at heart

parts.words: They're not bitter-mouthed, being bitter at heart
parts.note: the people meant never let bitter beer into their mouths, being teetotal, and the middle two letters of the word bitter are TT

explanation.surface: Sweet-natured people who nevertheless harbour resentment.
explanation.walkthrough: TT is the standard abbreviation for teetotal, and it sits at the heart of BITTER, a British style of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Teetotallers refuse alcohol, so no beer passes their lips.

clue.text: Continue asking-I like flowers

parts.note: to beg on is to keep on pleading
as means like, in the manner of

explanation.surface: Someone keeps pleading and admits a fondness for blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: These are popular garden and bedding plants grown for their blooms.

clue.text: "I —— with none" (Landor)

parts.note: the missing past-tense verb completes the first line of Walter Savage Landor's quatrain on his seventy-fifth birthday

explanation.surface: A gap to fill in a line of Victorian verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Landor's line runs 'I ... with none, for none was worth my strife'; the blank is a verb meaning fought or struggled.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet's word means fought or contended, the past of a verb of effort.

clue.text: They accommodate the hungry and their knives and forks

definitions.meaning: places such as works or school dining halls where food is served
sets of cutlery, usually in a fitted box

explanation.surface: Dining halls serve hungry people along with their cutlery.
explanation.definitionFit: Works dining rooms feed staff, and a fitted box of cutlery bears the same name.

clue.text: Educated? wrong, might one say?

indicators.note: asks the solver to voice the word for a legal wrong and hear another

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: Someone queries whether being educated is a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech the legal term for a civil wrong is said the same as the past of teach.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone schooled has been instructed, the past participle of teach.

clue.text: Opening of ruin

explanation.surface: The start of somebody's destruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfastening a knot is one sense, and a person's downfall is the other.

clue.text: All I get in difficult circumstances is the rope

indicators.note: the words All and I get inside the word for difficult circumstances

parts.note: hard as in hard times, tough going

explanation.surface: Someone in trouble finds all they receive is a hanging.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the hangman's rope; the answer is a sailor's rope for raising a sail.
explanation.definitionFit: A rope used on a ship to hoist a sail or flag, also spelt halyard.

clue.text: University champion full of well-brewed mead

indicators.note: the word for champion holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: an ace is a champion, an expert

indicators.note: mead is brewed up, its letters stirred into another order

explanation.surface: A university's champion drinker is full of good honey wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well-brewed' scrambles the honey wine, and those letters go between the C and E of the word for champion; the surface's mead-swilling scholar hides it.
explanation.definitionFit: The academic world of higher learning, the groves of academe.

clue.text: Read of new-style hat

indicators.note: Read of is given a new style, its letters set out in another order

explanation.surface: Someone reads about a fashionable new hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft felt hat with a creased crown and brim.

clue.text: At home to boring-sounding chap? Too kind!

parts.note: in means at home, not out

indicators.note: the word for boring is to be taken by its sound, losing a letter in the spelling

parts.note: dull means boring, tedious
a gent is a man, a chap

explanation.surface: Someone politely tells a dreary man who has visited that they are too generous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring-sounding' gives DUL, which sounds like DULL; the pieces said together sound like 'in dull gent'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being overly lenient or soft-hearted is to be too kind.

clue.text: A vibration causes a vessel to be partly open

parts.note: a jar is a jolt or shudder

explanation.surface: A jolt makes a pot spring partly open.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays it three ways: 'A vibration' is A JAR, so is 'a vessel', and joined up they leave a door slightly open.
explanation.definitionFit: A door left slightly open is said to be standing off the latch this way.

clue.text: Goddess of twin islands

indicators.note: the island abbreviation appears twice over, a pair

parts.note: IS is a map abbreviation for islands

explanation.surface: A deity worshipped on two islands.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian mother goddess, wife of Osiris.

clue.text: —— pursued by a bear in The Winter's Tale

definitions.text: —— pursued by a bear in The Winter's Tale

parts.words: —— pursued by a bear in The Winter's Tale
parts.note: the blank is the word of Shakespeare's most famous stage direction, for Antigonus leaving the stage

explanation.surface: A gap to fill in a famous Shakespeare stage direction.
explanation.walkthrough: Antigonus leaves the stage chased by a bear in Act 3 of The Winter's Tale.
explanation.definitionFit: The stage direction means a character leaves the stage, a departure.

clue.text: Amorous poetry, with singular beauty

parts.note: love lines are romantic verse
S is the grammar abbreviation for singular

explanation.surface: Romantic verse about one rare beauty.
explanation.definitionFit: Being lovely is attractiveness, the quality of being good to look at.

clue.text: Second-time herb

parts.note: an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A herb used for a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: A grey-leaved aromatic plant used in cooking, as in stuffing.

clue.text: Those training to succeed in test, cooking greens

parts.note: to pass is to succeed in an exam

indicators.note: the greens are being cooked up, their letters stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Trainee cooks hoping to pass an exam by preparing vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those training' are not trainees but people travelling on a train.
explanation.definitionFit: People riding on a train are travellers carried by it.
